subject: Computer Networking
title: How URLs Work
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: How URLs Work.

hook.text: Every page on the web has an address. URLs are the coordinates that take you to any resource online.

buildup.text: A URL has parts: scheme (https), host (example.com), path (/page), and optional query (?key=value).

discovery.text: The browser resolves the host to an IP via DNS, then uses the path to request a specific resource.

twist.text: Percent encoding handles special characters. A space becomes %20. That's why URLs look ugly sometimes.

climax.text: Fragment identifiers (#section) navigate within a page. They never leave the browser — the server never sees them.

punchline.text: URLs address every resource on the web. Simple, universal, powerful.

quiz.question: What part of a URL does the server never see?
options: The fragment identifier after the # symbol

details.summary: URLs provide a universal addressing scheme for every resource on the web, combining a protocol, domain name, path, and optional parameters into a single string. They enable direct linking to any page, image, or API endpoint on the internet with a human-readable and shareable format.
details.whyItMatters: URLs are one of the three foundational web technologies. Understanding their structure is essential for web development, SEO, API design, and debugging connectivity issues.
takeaways: URL components include scheme, domain, port, path, and query string
Path segments organize resources hierarchically on the server
Query parameters pass data in key-value pairs after the question mark

faq.question: What is the difference between a URL and a URI?
faq.answer: A URI is a universal resource identifier that uniquely names a resource. A URL is a type of URI that also specifies how to locate and access the resource using a protocol like HTTPS. In practice, the terms are used interchangeably for web addresses, but technically all URLs are URIs.

faq.question: What does URL encoding do?
faq.answer: URL encoding replaces unsafe characters with percent-encoded equivalents. Spaces become %20 or +. Special characters like & and = have reserved meanings in URLs. Encoding ensures that data passed in URLs does not break the URL structure.
